title: Unity
sub: A queue drained once per frame, the main-thread check and Awaitable (Unity 2023.1+, Unity 6)
cards/0/body:
At startup Unity installs a UnitySynchronizationContext on the main thread. It's simpler than the Dispatcher:

  • 1. Post adds the callback to a list under a lock. It can be called from any thread.
  • 2. Once per frame the player loop (the loop Unity runs every frame: input, Update, physics, rendering) takes the accumulated list on the main thread and runs everything in order.
  • 3. Anything added during that pass waits for the next frame.

So the continuation after awaiting a Task in a script runs on the main thread, but not immediately: at the next pass, up to a frame later.

And .Result on the main thread doesn't hang just the script, it hangs the whole game: the main thread is stuck, the frame never ends, the list is never drained, and the continuation .Result is waiting for never runs.
cards/1/title: Unity checks the thread, and whether the object is alive
cards/1/body:
Almost all of the Unity API (transform, GameObject, components, Instantiate) first checks that it was called from the main thread. Otherwise: UnityException: get_transform can only be called from the main thread (it starts with the name of the property or method you touched). From any thread you may only use what doesn't touch the engine: plain math (Vector3, Mathf) and your own C# objects.

Don't confuse it with MissingReferenceException. That one is about a destroyed object: the thread is right, but the object has already been destroyed (Destroy, a scene change). The C# reference is alive, but there's no engine object behind it: The object of type 'Transform' has been destroyed but you are still trying to access it. Why this happens with async is lesson 4.
cards/2/task: After an await with ConfigureAwait(false) the script moves the transform. Run it as is.
cards/3/explain: ConfigureAwait(false) sent the continuation to the pool, and transform checked the thread. MissingReferenceException is about a destroyed object, and the InvalidOperationException with that text comes from WPF.
cards/4/task: Fix it: the continuation must return to the main thread through the UnitySynchronizationContext queue.
cards/5/task: Unity can hang too. Drive it into a deadlock.
cards/6/q: Why does .Result in Start freeze the whole game and not just this script?
cards/6/options/0: The main thread is stuck on .Result: the frame never ends, so there's no Update, no rendering and no draining of the context queue
cards/6/options/1: Unity suspends every pool thread while a script waits for a task
cards/6/options/2: UnitySynchronizationContext holds network replies until the end of the frame
cards/6/explain: The main thread drives the frame. While it's stuck, everything is stuck, including the queue where the continuation .Result needs is waiting.
cards/7/body:
Since Unity 2023.1 (and in Unity 6) an async method can return Awaitable instead of Task: a Unity class built for the game loop. Two main differences from Task:

  • 1. A continuation without a queue. In Unity, a Task brings its continuation back through UnitySynchronizationContext, up to a frame later. An Awaitable runs the continuation synchronously, at the moment the wait completes: waiting for the next frame resumes right in that frame, with no extra round trip.
  • 2. Pooled instances. To avoid creating an object per wait, Unity takes Awaitables from a pool and returns them there after completion. That's why you may await one Awaitable only once: by the second await the instance may already belong to another operation. Unity calls this undefined behavior: sometimes an exception, sometimes a hang.

It's the same rule as for ValueTask (u3.l3), for the same reason: the object is reused. If several places need the result, keep the result itself or wrap the call in an async Task: a Task can be awaited any number of times.
cards/8/body:
Static Awaitable methods replace coroutine yield instructions and switch threads:

  • Awaitable.NextFrameAsync(): resume in the next frame;
  • Awaitable.EndOfFrameAsync(): at the end of the current frame, after rendering;
  • Awaitable.FixedUpdateAsync(): at the next physics step;
  • Awaitable.WaitForSecondsAsync(s): after s seconds;
  • Awaitable.FromAsyncOperation(op): when a Unity AsyncOperation finishes: loading a scene or an asset;
  • Awaitable.BackgroundThreadAsync(): resume on a pool thread;
  • Awaitable.MainThreadAsync(): return to the main thread (if already there, immediately, without a pause).

The frame, seconds and AsyncOperation waits also accept a CancellationToken (lesson 4). Between BackgroundThreadAsync and MainThreadAsync the code runs on the pool: you can't touch the Unity API there, or you get the same UnityException.
cards/9/q: Compute in the background, then move the object
cards/9/explain: Without MainThreadAsync the transform line runs on the pool and fails with UnityException.
cards/10/q: Unity 6. A script on the main thread does await Task.Delay(100) and then moves the transform. Where and when does the transform line run?
cards/10/options/0: On the main thread, at the next pass over the UnitySynchronizationContext queue: up to a frame after Delay completed
cards/10/options/1: On the timer thread, right after 100 ms, and it fails with UnityException
cards/10/options/2: On the main thread, synchronously at the moment Delay completes, in the middle of the current Update
cards/10/explain: A Task brings its continuation back through Post into UnitySynchronizationContext, and the queue is drained once per frame. Resuming synchronously, without a queue, is what Awaitable does.
cards/11/q: Unity 6. What's wrong with this code?
cards/11/options/0: A second await of the same Awaitable: the instance may be back in the pool and belong to another operation
cards/11/options/1: Nothing: the second await returns the finished result right away, like with Task
cards/11/options/2: A second await is only allowed after MainThreadAsync
cards/11/explain: One Awaitable, one await. If you need the result again, use the saved level or wrap the call in an async Task.
